transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-11
Time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Daniel Park (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Liam O'Neill (Aurora Head of ML), Priya Rao (Aurora Platform), Sara Gomez (Aurora PM)

Summary (auto-gen, may be rough): Reviewed benchmark runs, caching shows ~20-30% token savings for chat flows with repeated prefixes. Batching gives 2-2.8x throughput but adds tail latency. Action items listed.

00:00 - Speaker 1 (Daniel): "All right hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda: go over the tokens per dollar runs we shipped yesterday, caching results, and then batching tradeoffs, and close with next steps. sound good?"
00:18 - Speaker 2 (Liam): "Yep sounds good. thanks Dan. we pulled the run overnight, excited to see the numbers."
00:35 - Daniel: "Cool. Maya you want to start with the benchmark highlights?"
00:40 - Maya: "Yeah, sure. so I pulled the baseline from last week, that's our default hosted setup on the 16k context model, running with no caching and 1 request per batch. baseline tokens per second is around 140 tokens/sec on avg, cost estimate about $0.0065 per 1k tokens with our current model variant... well that's from the spreadsheet, might be a little off in the auto transcription."
01:05 - Priya: "When you say 140 tokens/sec, that's per GPU or per node right?"
01:10 - Maya: "Per node for the dedicated pool we used in the test. but throughput scales with batching so bear with me. baseline cost is baseline hosted price - again approximate."
01:25 - Sara: "Can you quickly restate what our target is? Liam said we wanted sub-200ms median latency and cost under X per 10k customer interactions? I'm trying to remember the exact number."
01:36 - Liam: "Yeah target is median latency <200ms for the 1-turn chat flows, and cost around $0.50 per 10k interactions as a ballpark for this pilot."
01:50 - Daniel: "Okay good to have that. so caching: we ran prefix (semi-static) caching on the common product description prompts. that reduced emitted tokens by roughly 22% across the sampled flows, and end-to-end tokens/sec per dollar improved from about 140 tokens/sec per node to ~175 tokens/sec effective when you account for fewer tokens generated — so roughly a 25% cost improvement."
02:18 - Liam: "22% seems great. was that for both retrieval+prompt or just prompt prefix?"
02:24 - Maya: "Mostly prefix. we saw an additional hit when we combined with short-term KV caching for session state — that added another 5-7% savings in certain user journeys. so combined about 27-29% total in best cases. note there are diminishing returns on very dynamic prompts."
02:45 - Priya: "How accurate are those numbers? like real production distribution will be noisier."
02:50 - Maya: "They're from a 6-hour run on representative traffic we recorded; transcription note — some of the endpoint names in the logs were munged, but raw token counts are in the sheet. quality is medium but the numbers are stable across samples."
03:05 - Sara: "What about batching? I know more batching gives lower cost but raises latency."
03:11 - Maya: "Right. we ran batching experiments at batch sizes 1 (baseline), 4, 8 and 16. throughput in tokens/sec increased roughly 1x, 1.9x, 2.4x and 2.8x respectively on average. however median latency moved from 140ms at batch size 1 to 190ms at batch size 4, 260ms at 8, and 340ms at 16. tails got worse. so for your latency SLO (<200ms) you could push to batch size 4 safely, maybe 6 depending on peeks, to get roughly 1.8-2.1x throughput improvement with acceptable median."
03:47 - Liam: "So if we take batch size 4 and enable caching we get both wins? any conflicts?"
03:52 - Maya: "Yes they combine. caching reduces tokens per request, which changes the batch composition a little but overall we still see the batching multiplier. combining batch 4 + caching we measured effective tokens/sec per dollar improvement of about 3.1x over baseline no-cache, batch1."
04:09 - Daniel: "We put that into the cost model spreadsheet as an "effective tokens/$" row — I'll share the sheet after the call. note this is with our current quantized 4-bit variant; if you switch to a cheaper 4-bit compiled kernel or a 3-bit variant you can potentially push cost down another 15-25% but with risk of small quality regressions."
04:36 - Priya: "Can you remind us what quality checks we need if we change quantization? we have to avoid product hallucinations."
04:41 - Maya: "Yes, good point. we run the eval suite we shipped — the Redwood eval harness — on a sampled prompt set and track rouge-ish metrics plus a handful of LLM-specific QA checks. we'll re-run that if you want a quantization delta. typically changes are small but we flag any regression > 1.5% on key metrics."
04:58 - Sara: "Any thoughts on routing between hosted and dedicated? we may want to keep high-risk queries on dedicated or private."
05:05 - Daniel: "Routing policy is straightforward — we can mark sensitive traffic to always go to your VPC/dedicated pool. that will change cost because dedicated pricing is different but you get isolation. Priya is standing up a VPC lab for the SE deep dive right?"
05:16 - Priya: "Yes I'll try to have a small test cluster up by Monday. probably minimal capacity, just for routing and debug."
05:22 - Liam: "For the cost model, can you show tokens/sec per dollar as a single KPI? that helps execs."
05:28 - Daniel: "Yep. in the sheet I put an "tokens_per_$" metric, so higher is better. baseline was ~21k tokens per dollar, combined batch+cache was ~64k tokens per dollar in our test — that's the 3x improvement Maya mentioned. Again these numbers assume your request distribution from the sample."
05:46 - Maya: "I want to call out a nuance: prefix caching can cause slightly higher request fan-outs if you have many short prompts that share prefix, because backend cache expiry and cache warm time matter. so initial cold-start will see less savings. Over time with steady traffic it stabilizes."
06:05 - Sara: "Do we need a warm-up period for the pilot?"
06:08 - Maya: "Yes, recommend 24-72 hours for stable caching numbers. that's why we suggested a 24h caching-enabled run next."
06:14 - Liam: "Okay let's schedule the 24h run. Maya can you run it against our recorded traffic?"
06:18 - Maya: "Yep I can. I'll run it in Redwood Dedicated staged pool simulating your QPS, with caching turned on. will capture raw token logs and cost delta."
06:25 - Daniel: "Perf question from Priya earlier — how much infra memory does the KV cache need? we worry about memory pressure."
06:31 - Maya: "Depends on number of cached prefixes and average prompt length. for your catalog we estimate ~2-4GB for the hot set in our tests. could be more if you cache whole embeddings or long context. we'll provide guidance in the run notes."
06:45 - Priya: "That's fine but we need to know sizing for our VPC cluster."
06:49 - Maya: "We'll include a memory sizing table."
06:52 - Daniel: "Any concerns about compliance or audit logs with caching? Liam?"
06:56 - Liam: "As long as audit logs show cache hits/misses and cached item keys are hashed and not storing PII it's fine. We have to add that to the security checklist."
07:08 - Maya: "Redwood tracks cache metrics and access logs; we can provide masked logs and an audit trail. Also SSO and SAML are already set for your account."
07:18 - Sara: "One more thing: the user flows with retrieval (RAG) — does that change tokens-per-dollar calculations much?"
07:25 - Maya: "RAG increases tokens emitted sometimes because retrieval adds context; however if you cache retrieved chunks for similar queries you get savings. in our RAG sample the net effect was neutral to slightly positive when combined with prefix caching because you avoid re-retrieving the same pages."
07:45 - Daniel: "Let's talk timeline: Maya will run 24h caching run; Priya will stand up VPC test cluster; Daniel will share spreadsheet; and we'll do an infra deep-dive next week to tune batching and routing. Any blockers?"
07:57 - Priya: "No blockers. I'll need access instructions from SE for the VPC link."
08:02 - Maya: "I'll send step-by-step and a minimal cloud-init to provision the test node."
08:08 - Liam: "One last question on pricing: is there an option for committed reserved capacity to get lower unit price during peak?"
08:14 - Daniel: "Yes, Redwood Dedicated has reserved capacity pricing with monthly commits; we can model that in the spreadsheet too. we'll show a committed vs on-demand delta."
08:25 - Sara: "For our exec summary we want a single slide: current baseline vs projected after cache+batch+commit."
08:31 - Daniel: "Will do. I'll draft that slide and share with Sara."
08:36 - Maya: "I'll also include the quantization sensitivity run and the eval delta."
08:40 - Liam: "Perfect. thanks everyone."
08:43 - Daniel: "Ok we'll wrap. next sync same time next week unless we need more frequent check-ins during the 24h run. closing notes: action items are in the doc. thanks all."

End of transcript.
